entries.title: A Normie Democrat Revolt Is Pushing Abdul El-Sayed Toward Victory
entries.summary: “The only reasonable thing seems to be: Burn it down and start over, and make it different,” one Michigan organizer said.
entries.content:
WILLIAMSTON, Mich. — Kent Tisdale spent most of his life voting for Republicans before he started voting for Democrats, even backing Donald Trump in 2016. The 70-year-old retiree can even remember that his biggest concern backing Mitt Romney in 2012 was that the GOP presidential nominee wasn’t conservative enough.

He is now seriously considering supporting Abdul El-Sayed in Tuesday’s Senate Democratic primary.

Tisdale, now a member of his local Indivisible chapter, said Trump’s presidency and the deluge of money in politics led him to El-Sayed, whose passion has impressed him even if the candidate’s politics are further left than he’d like.

“I don’t feel I’ve changed that much,” said Tisdale, who spoke to NOTUS while attending an event for a local House candidate. “But I feel the environment has changed.”

In Michigan and across the country this year, voters like Tisdale are transforming Democratic primaries — and potentially putting the party on a different path as it heads into the 2028 presidential campaign.

Rank-and-file Democratic voters who once naturally inclined toward establishment-backed candidates are instead supporting — or at least showing an openness to — lefty candidates they would have previously believed to be outside the political mainstream. They’re driven by disappointment in old-guard Democrats’ inability to beat Trump in 2024 and a growing sense that the country’s politics need a fresh direction.

It’s that change in the electorate that, more than anything this year, explains why El-Sayed is now favored to beat Rep. Haley Stevens in Tuesday’s Senate primary in Michigan. Stevens is running the type of campaign — backed by key party endorsements, support in the Black community and plenty of money — that has helped centrist Democrats like her defeat progressive challengers for years. That pattern held for Hillary Clinton in 2016 and Joe Biden in 2020.

But the voters on the receiving end of that effort are in a much different place than they were in 2024, much less 2018 or 2016.

“So many people feel the same way I do, that something needs to be done,” said Jan Cohen, who founded a local Indivisible chapter last year. “And the only reasonable thing seems to be: Burn it down and start over, and make it different. We have to take the stands and do everything we can.”



Cohen voted against El-Sayed in 2018 when he ran for governor against Gretchen Whitmer. But she said she’s grown frustrated with Michigan Democratic leaders recently, worried they no longer seem to be pushing progressive policy through the state and upset at their support for Stevens.

The frustration normie Democratic voters feel with their own party is in part responsible for the defeat of establishment-backed politicians like Janet Mills in Maine’s Senate race, or the handful of defeats of Democratic incumbents in safe blue House seats. In nearby Wisconsin, Democratic voters look poised to nominate a democratic socialist for governor in that state’s open gubernatorial race despite protests from party leaders like Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers.

El-Sayed, a former Wayne County, Michigan, health director, earned just 30% of the vote against Whitmer in 2018. That sort of defeat had become the norm for progressive Democrats, most crucially during each of Sen. Bernie Sanders’ presidential campaigns. In those races, the senator from Vermont was unable to break through with many middle-of-the-road Democratic voters, especially in the Black community, and was ultimately pushed back by a party establishment that emphasized electability and realistic policy goals.

Polls now show El-Sayed in a strong position ahead of Tuesday’s primary, leading Stevens by a double-digit margin in a spate of recent surveys, despite tens of millions of dollars spent against his campaign by outside groups.

Stevens officials maintain the congresswoman has a chance to win Tuesday, dismissing polls as underestimating the support of her core voters. Some of the frustrated voters, including Tisdale, have also not actually made up their minds despite their openness to El-Sayed, expressing some reservations about his ideology and electability in the fall.

And even progressive activists say privately they think the movement of these voters toward candidates like El-Sayed is less about a newfound acceptance of lefty policy platforms like single-payer health care and more about their anger with the Democratic establishment.

Some Stevens supporters acknowledge that El-Sayed has tapped into a deep frustration in the party, pushing his candidacy to a stronger position than many expected was once possible for a candidate with his politics.

“Abdul has drafted behind that uneasiness with our party,” said Lon Johnson, a veteran Democratic strategist in the state. “He has done a good job of drafting behind it, and corralling it.”

“This year is very, very different than 2024,” said another Democratic strategist supportive of Stevens’ campaign, granted anonymity to speak candidly. “And I don’t like what that means for our party’s prospects, but that’s the way it’s going. People are pissed.”

In a gaggle with reporters after a campaign event last week, El-Sayed said he personally had changed a lot since his 2018 race, noting he’s gone from a 32-year-old first-time candidate to a 41-year-old with two kids. He said he believes his message resonates much more deeply with the electorate now than it did then.

“The bigger change is not really me,” he said. “The broader public has come through a lot. In the ensuing eight years, we’ve had a pandemic. We’ve lived through one full Trump presidency and then another quarter of one. We’ve watched an inflation crisis. And the central point that I was making is that Trump is not the disease, he’s the symptom. And I think this time around, after his ... first reelection, I think people understand that.

“There’s something about having been saying the same thing for the better part of 10 years, since I jumped into public service,” he said.

El-Sayed said he didn’t think the party’s failure to defeat Trump in 2024 was the root of voters’ frustration, instead blaming the simmering rage on Democrats’ inability to make people’s lives easier in tangible ways.

El-Sayed’s pitch to voters hasn’t deviated this campaign. Before talking to reporters last week, he rallied with supporters in Lansing with a message focused on Israel’s wrongdoing in the Middle East, a single-payer health care system and a vow to take money out of politics. His final campaign ads feature progressive leaders like Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York).

“I want you to remember that you're walking the same exact path as all of those folks who fought for everything coming from abolition to native rights to women’s suffrage to LGBTQ rights to religious freedom to ending Jim Crow, to building an America where we had unions, the folks who showed up to sit down and stand up for rights, the folks who gave us Medicare and Medicaid,” El-Sayed told supporters last week in Ypsilanti. “You are walking that path.”

Polls indicate that El-Sayed still has some of the same struggles that have traditionally plagued progressives, especially with middle-aged and elderly Black voters. Stevens is counting on their support, along with older white union voters, to give her a chance at victory, and has developed her campaign to win them over.

But Democrats say that many suburban voters who once considered themselves ideologically and temperamentally moderate before Trump’s victory in 2024 have entered their own state of rebellion. Their anger can be harshest for candidates like Stevens, Democrats say, who was first elected in 2018 but hasn’t been able to stop the GOP’s advance since entering office.

“The base is so angry at normal Democrats who were around back then and are exactly the people who said, ‘We’ve got this,’” said a second Democratic strategist, granted anonymity to speak candidly. “And they didn’t.”

Tisdale, a resident of Williamston, is still interested in candidates with more centrist politics, too: He spoke to NOTUS here at a meet-and-greet event for Matt Maasdam, a moderate Democrat running in the state’s 7th Congressional District. (Maasdam and Bridget Brink, another candidate with the support of local Democrats, are both in danger of losing to a progressive activist.)

But even as a man who said he’s never voted for Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin, despite living in her old House district, Tisdale said El-Sayed’s “passion level” might give Democrats a needed jolt to take on Trump. It’s why he says he and others, including his wife, are considering voting for the insurgent.

“We think that kind of energy is how you fight back,” he said.

entries.title: DSA Wants to Abolish the Senate. Bernie Sanders Says 'No.'
entries.summary: Democrats across the caucus dismissed the idea of restructuring Congress.
entries.content:
Democratic Socialists of America, a group that’s gaining momentum across the country, is pushing to scrap the U.S. Senate and replace it with a unicameral legislature. Senate Democrats aren’t on board.

“It's in the Constitution, and it is a critical component of the United States government to pass legislation with the House,” Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly told NOTUS. “In my view, that is not a serious recommendation.”

“I don't even know what they mean by that. I don’t have any idea,” added a befuddled Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren.

Even Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent who’s long called himself a democratic socialist, isn’t on board with the proposal.

“No,” Sanders told NOTUS. He declined to elaborate, saying he had a flight to catch.

The DSA’s new platform, unveiled earlier this month, calls for expanding the social safety net and making sweeping changes to the federal government. Those include abolishing the Senate, the presidency, and the Supreme Court. Those institutions would be replaced with an “executive and judiciary chosen by and subordinate to Congress,” as well as an expanded House of Representatives with multiple political parties instead of the current two-party system. Those ideas would require approving an amendment to the U.S. Constitution, a major hurdle in a polarized political environment.

“The Senate is a very undemocratic institution,” Ashik Siddique, co-chair of the Democratic Socialists of America, said in an interview on C-SPAN. “I talked a bit about democracy, a small ‘d’ democracy, and that’s really important to us. We want democratic representation of all people who live in this country.”

The DSA platform, titled “Workers Deserve More,” has drawn attacks and ridicule from top Republicans who are seeking to tie some of its controversial ideas, such as abolishing the police, to the Democratic Party and its candidates ahead of November’s midterm elections. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist and front-runner in the Wisconsin governor’s Democratic primary race, for example, is facing questions about the platform and her past comments calling to abolish the police.

“I do not support the full platform of the national DSA, and I am not endorsed by DSA national. What democratic socialism is, is a form of government that puts working-class people first,” Hong said in a debate last week, backing away from a 2020 social media post in which she called to abolish the police.

Some Democrats believe their party isn’t doing enough to marginalize the democratic socialist movement, which recently claimed victories in local and congressional races in New York, Pennsylvania, Colorado and Washington, D.C. According to a recent CNN poll, about a third of Democrats now identify as democratic socialists.

“These people sat in a room and said, ‘How much crazy shit can we cram into a platform?’ Like, ‘Yeah, abolish the Senate? Sure, why not. Hey, abolish the presidency? Yeah, sure, why not?’ That's crazy shit,” Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman, who has broken with Democrats on several key issues, told NOTUS. “I'm unique, I'm the only Democrat that will call it out.”

But other Democrats downplayed the rise of DSA, arguing that most people who consider themselves to be far-left progressives ascribe to more popular ideas like taxing the rich and providing universal health care.

“I know people in Richmond who align with DSA who don't want to abolish the Senate,” said Virginia Sen. Tim Kaine. “They don't want to abolish the presidency. If you ask them, ‘Why are you DSA?’ they will say, ‘I'm a Democrat, but I like DSA because I don't like the concentration of wealth.’”

New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker said his constituents are more concerned about their economic situation and having health care rather than “proposing things that would require a constitutional amendment,” which he called “farcical at this point.”

Still, Booker, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential candidate, said he did support other structural reforms such as granting statehood to Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico, as well as changing equal state apportionment, which gives every state two senators, no matter its population.

“The Senate does have things that our founders never imagined, like the fact that North Dakota, South Dakota, Wyoming, Idaho and Montana have 10 senators and they have less population than Los Angeles County, and that's really problematic,” Booker said. “But there are things that really focus on the real issues of people that we can get done here, that I think we should be organizing around.”

Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, meanwhile, argued that voter frustration with how the Senate operates could be addressed if its members stood up for the system of checks and balances as laid out in the U.S. Constitution.

“I think that we need to do something about a supine Senate. There’s a lot of madness happening right now in the White House that this body could do something to address if there was any courage,” Warnock said, before adding, “If my Republican colleagues had any moral courage.”

entries.title: Sen. Bernie Moreno Says His Ex-Son-In-Law, Rep. Max Miller, ‘Shouldn’t Serve in the House’
entries.summary: Miller earlier Sunday defended himself in a livestream against domestic abuse allegations from his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, the senator’s daughter.
entries.content:
Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno said Sunday that his former son-in-law, Rep. Max Miller, should seek professional help and should not serve in Congress, citing allegations of domestic abuse against his daughter and granddaughter.

“If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them. He should not serve in the House of Representatives,” Moreno wrote on X. “I believe Max Miller needs to seek professional help to end the clear pattern of abuse he has left in his wake. I believe he should not be free to continue endangering others until he does.”

Miller, a fellow Ohio Republican, reaffirmed his plans to seek reelection in a livestream on X earlier Sunday and denied the allegations of abuse from his ex-wife, Emily Moreno.

The two-term congressman released files containing court documents, text messages, audio recordings and videos that he says back up his side of the ongoing dispute.

“My former wife is engaging in a pattern of reporting incredible, serious and destructive allegations with absolutely no evidence,” Miller said on the livestream.

“God bless you all,” Miller said later, directing people to view files he’d shared on Dropbox. “I'm not getting out of this race, and I'm winning in November, and I'll be back in the 120th” congressional session.

Miller’s Sunday pushback comes as his reelection chances could be dimming.

A poll conducted by a Republican firm Wednesday and Thursday and reviewed by NOTUS showed Miller underwater in his district. His Democratic opponent in Ohio’s 7th Congressional District, Brian Poindexter, was up 5 percentage points, polling at 44% to Miller’s 39% with 16% undecided. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.8 percentage points.

His favorability rating was also down, with 41% of voters viewing him unfavorably and only 25% holding a favorable view. Some 22% were unsure and 12% had never heard of him.

Emily Moreno and Miller were married from 2022 to 2025. The couple have one daughter. The domestic abuse allegations surfaced in May, complicating Miller’s reelection bid in the midterms that will determine which party controls Congress.

“It is shameful that Max Miller decided to go on a bizarre and lie-filled rant about his ex-wife to desperately try to save his political career,” Stefan Mychajliw, a spokesperson for Emily Moreno, wrote in a statement posted after the livestream. “No loving parent would have ever used their daughter as a PR pawn to save their own political career. Miller can lie and spin on X, but he cannot do so under oath in a court of law. We are confident that justice will prevail in court.”

Emily Moreno asked the court on Thursday to issue a restraining order against Miller preventing him from contacting her lawyer Andrew Zashin, alleging the congressman had physical and verbal altercations with Zashin.

During their marriage, Miller allegedly threw hot or scalding water at Emily Moreno during an argument which caused burns to her body, according to court filings in the legal battle. Emily Moreno also said in court filings that Miller shoved her against a wall during one confrontation and another time held a gun to her head. Miller has denied all of the allegations.

“It was horseplay in our kitchen,” Miller said Sunday about the hot water incident. “I sprayed water at her from the sprayer attached to our kitchen sink tap water, which does not reach boiling temperature or scalding.”

Mother Jones reported last month that Emily Moreno said she could not rule out the possibility that Miller caused their daughter's broken collarbone due to his alleged history of violence toward her.

Miller on Sunday disputed that account.

“I had dropped my daughter off with my former wife before that injury was even discovered,” Miller said. “She was not in my care during that time, and when I found out about her injury, I canceled my trip to Florida to be there for her while she recovered.”

Sen. Moreno, who told NOTUS last week that “I don’t know” if Miller should be replaced on the ticket, said Sunday on X that he is seriously concerned whenever Miller is watching his grandchild.

“He is a danger to my daughter, and I hold my breath every minute he has custody of my granddaughter,” Bernie Moreno wrote.

Miller said Emily Moreno has “struggled with significant mental health challenges,” and he said he believes it has contributed to the allegations against him.

Miller’s X account posted a link to Dropbox with a slew of files, though the link was quickly deleted. The congressman blamed the website, and said the files were not made using congressional resources: “Just to be clear: these documents were produced by my personal attorneys and paid for by me directly.” He posted the files again later Sunday morning.

Emily Moreno’s comments about Miller aren’t the first allegations of domestic abuse the Ohio congressman has faced.

Miller, who served as an aide to President Donald Trump in his first term, dated White House press secretary Stephanie Grisham in 2020. After their relationship ended, Grisham published an opinion piece in The Washington Post describing abuse she allegedly endured from a former partner who was not named in the piece, but whom Grisham later identified as Miller. He denied the allegations, arguing they coincided with the release of her memoir.

Miller sued Grisham for defamation in 2021, and they reached a confidential settlement in 2023. Grisham recently sued Miller, claiming he broke the terms of the settlement by speaking publicly about the case.

This story has been updated to include a statement from Emily Moreno's spokesperson and new polling information.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin, Reese Gorman

entries.title: Rep. Marcy Kaptur Hospitalized After Hit-and-Run Crash in Ohio
entries.summary: A witness says the other driver fled in another vehicle as police report an “active and ongoing” investigation.
entries.content:
Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur was hospitalized following a hit-and-run car crash in her home state of Ohio on Sunday morning, according to the Toledo Police Department.

The crash occurred around 10:45 a.m. in Toledo, and two people were taken to the hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, police said. It was unclear who the second person was.

"This morning Congresswoman Kaptur was a passenger in a vehicle on her way to a church service when the car she was traveling in was struck,” Kaptur’s office wrote in a statement. “She is active, alert, and being treated for non-life threatening injuries.”

Toledo police described the investigation as “active and ongoing" and did not immediately say whether any suspect had been apprehended.

Local news station WTOL 11 published photos from the scene showing two damaged vehicles. One witness told WTOL that the other driver was picked up by another vehicle and fled shortly after the incident.

Kaptur’s colleagues shared messages of support on X.

“Tina and I are praying for a quick and full recovery for @RepMarcyKaptur,” Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) wrote. “We hope the person responsible for this reckless act is apprehended quickly and held accountable.”

“I'm praying for my colleague @RepMarcyKaptur after her crash this morning,” Rep. Andy Biggs (R-Arizona) posted. “May she be restored to full health in short order.”

Kaptur is running for reelection for Ohio’s 9th Congressional District. She is set to face former state Rep. Derek Merrin in November. Merrin asked followers to help him in “praying for her speedy recovery.”

This is a developing story and will be updated.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin
